then.text: Still filling that notebook? Good. Economics is mostly noticing things, then counting them.
Derek and his pint! Prices up, pounds down. He's been telling that story since before I was born, and he's right every time.
That's the secret. None of it is magic. It's people, choices and sums.
Here, on me. The opportunity cost was a chat with the fishmonger, and I can afford it.
Whitelock's is just off Briggate. Derek's the one who remembers Decimal Day. Ask him about the price of a pint.

else.text: Dr Akhtar. I teach economics up the road, and I come here to watch it happen.
Michael Marks opened a penny stall in this market in 1884. Nothing over a penny, no haggling. People loved knowing where they stood.
A puzzle. Two stalls. Mags can make six pies or three scarves a day. Tom can make two pies or two scarves.
Mags is better at both. So who should knit the scarves?

then.text: Right. A scarf costs Mags two pies she could have baked, and costs Tom only one.

else.text: Count the cost in pies. Every scarf Mags knits costs her two pies. Every scarf Tom knits costs him one.
So Tom knits, Mags bakes, and they swap. Between them there are more pies and more scarves than if each did both.
That's comparative advantage. David Ricardo, 1817. It's why towns specialise, and why carrying jute from Dundee pays.
Start an Economist's notebook. It's in your Almanac now, and it'll fill as you go: markets, the Building Society, even the casino.
Next, find Derek in Whitelock's. Ask him what a pint has to do with inflation.

then.text: {greeting} The display's up by the clock. People come and look, then buy a penny chew. History in action.
A toy knight from the Armouries, a fleece from Kirkstall and a pill tin from the Thackray. That's Leeds in a box, that.
Marks started with a tray round his neck and a penny sign. This'll go by the clock where his stall stood. Here, something for your trouble.
That Bobbin's been living in the old wool stall since the 1970s. It wants to see the world. Or at least Bradford.

else.text: Still need summat from the Thackray Museum, up the top end past Briggate. Something medical. Nothing squelchy.
Still need summat from Kirkstall Abbey, over the river. The monks were wool men, like this market.
Still need summat from the Royal Armouries down by the dock. Mind the armourer, he likes a scrap.
{greeting} You're stood near where Marks and Spencer began. Michael Marks, 1884, a stall and a sign: Don't ask the price, it's a penny.
We're doing a display for the market's birthday. Leeds in a box. I need three things: something from the Royal Armouries, something from Kirkstall Abbey, and something from the Thackray Museum.
Off you pop. And don't ask the price. It's a favour.

kirkgate_butcher.text: {greeting} Butchers' Row used to be all one long line of us. Tripe, pies, black pudding. Now try saying 'no thanks' to a pork pie in a Leeds accent.

kirkgate_fish.text: {greeting} Haddock, not cod, round here. And chips in beef dripping if you go to the right chippy. Don't tell the vegetarians.

hall_stallholder.text: Now then. Fruit, veg, a pound of tripe, a toy knight. Kirkgate sells everything, lad.
Show us what you've got and I'll tell you what it's worth. Honest.
Mind how you go. And buy something from the bazaar, it keeps the pigeons honest.
